definition: A measure of how certain a model is in its own prediction or output, often derived from output probabilities but not always well-calibrated to actual correctness.
details: Model confidence is an important but imperfect signal; well-known calibration issues mean a model's stated or implied confidence doesn't always accurately reflect the true likelihood that its output is correct.

explainer.lead: A measure of how certain a model is in its own prediction or output, often derived from output probabilities. It matters because it is an important but imperfect signal.

tiers.eli5: It is the model saying how sure it feels, which is not the same as actually being right.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use confidence to gate decisions and route uncertain cases to review. A pitfall is well-known calibration issues: stated or implied confidence does not always reflect the true likelihood of correctness.
tiers.paperLevel: Usually derived from output probabilities; calibration issues mean confidence is not always well-calibrated to actual correctness.

explainer.example: A model reports high confidence on a prediction that turns out wrong, showing confidence and correctness diverged.
